schools.summary: Gill notes that Hannah had prayed before, but silently, and this is vocal; she had been answered and now gives thanks, thanksgiving being itself a kind of prayer, which is why the narrative calls a song a prayer. He cites the Targum for a spirit of prophecy and reports that the Jews reckon her one of the seven prophetesses, finding in the song not only her own experience of divine goodness but things to be done hereafter in Israel, and particularly the Messiah.

Henry makes most of the fact that a thanksgiving is called a prayer: thanksgiving is an essential part of prayer, and in every address to God we must express a grateful regard to him as our benefactor; what we win by prayer we may wear with comfort, and must wear with praise, and thanks for mercies received shall be accepted as a petition for further mercy. He observes that she does not commend Samuel for the prettiest child or the most toward for his age, as fond parents are apt to do, but overlooks the gift and praises the giver — there may be other Samuels, he says, but no other Jehovah. Four attributes are celebrated in the opening lines on his reckoning: unspotted purity, almighty power, unsearchable wisdom and unerring justice. On the horn he hears music rather than cattle, David's singers having been appointed to lift up the horn, so that the phrase means her praises are raised to an unusual strain; and the song stands on record, he adds, to encourage those of the weaker sex to attend the throne of grace.

Clarke calls the hymn an oracular declaration rather than a prayer, every part having respect to the future, and quotes Hales, who finds it excelling in simplicity and uniformity of sentiment, exalting the humble-minded and abasing the arrogant, and ranks Hannah a prophetess of the first class for describing the promised Saviour as a King before there was any king in Israel, and for first applying the epithet which is Messiah in Hebrew, Christ in Greek and Anointed in English. Kimchi, he adds, was so struck by the language that he ingenuously confessed the King of whom Hannah speaks is the Messiah. He notes that the best manuscripts write the hymn in poetic lines, and prints it so, judging from the connection that she delivered it at her son's dedication rather than at his birth; he agrees that horn means power and dominion and finds the sentiment among the heathen too, quoting Horace, who tells his wine-jar that it adds strength and horns to the poor man. Wesley adds that she shows her modesty by not naming Peninnah, only her enemies in general.

Keil calls the psalm the mature fruit of the Spirit of God, and says the pious woman discerned in her own experience the general laws of the divine economy; what she had known of God's gracious government while bowed down was a pledge that the nation, then deeply oppressed, would likewise be lifted up. Ellicott makes the movement personal first: she had been an unhappy woman, her life as she thought a failure and her dearest hopes baffled, and had fled to the Rock of Israel and found rest, and then joy, the hymn afterwards becoming one of the loved songs of the people, handed down in the words that first fell from her. He also cautions against a misreading of her boast — mine horn is exalted does not mean I am proud but I am strong, mighty now in the gift received, the image coming from oxen and grown familiar to a shepherd-people.

debates.question: Does mine horn is exalted claim strength or boast of pride?

sides.position: strength and dominion — the figure is from oxen, and the heathen used it the same way
music — David’s singers lifted up the horn, so her praises are raised to an unusual strain

themes: my heart rejoiceth in the Lord
mine horn is exalted in the Lord
thanksgiving as an essential part of prayer
the song as prophecy of the Messiah

2.pericope_label: The perfections of God and the reversals of providence

schools.summary: Gill piles up adverbs on the holiness: God is essentially, originally, independently, perfectly and immutably holy, as others are not. Angels are holy, but not of themselves, and cover their faces while celebrating that perfection; nor is theirs naturally unchangeable, as the fall of some demonstrates. Among men some were holy only in a typical sense, some outwardly before others but not before God, and even in the truly sanctified there is a likeness only. He takes the warning against proud talk to address Peninnah and her allies, whose mouths would now be stopped.

Clarke turns the claim outward: holiness is peculiar to the God of Israel, and no false god ever pretended to it, nor any religion professed before the true revelation. On the rock he reports Rabbi Maimon's observation that the word, applied to Jehovah, means fountain or spring, and concludes that no source of continual help exists but our God. Of the closing verb he renders it that actions are directed, drawing from that how by his counsel alone can we begin, continue or end any work; and he reports the Targum's reading of the reversals as a series of prophecies, against the Philistines, Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar, the Greeks and Haman, while thinking for himself that these things frequently happen in the ordinary course, and that it is the particular providence of God which Hannah celebrates through this simple yet sublime ode. Wesley puts the holiness briefly — none is holy besides God, save by participation — reduces the rock to comfort, and takes seven for many, hearing the prophetic style in the past put for the future.

Keil explains why the reason given is that there is none beside him: holiness is simply the moral reflection of the glory of the one absolute God, so that the wicked should tremble before it rather than boast of lofty things. He glosses the barren bearing seven, that being the full number of the divine blessing, while the mother of many pines away, having lost her sons and with them her support in old age. Ellicott keeps the rock a stone and traces the image to the desert wandering, where the strange fantastic crags of Sinai, standing up amid shifting sands, supplied a picture of unchangeableness and security; the term is first found in the Song of Moses, where the juxtaposition of rock and salvation suggests Hannah knew that national hymn. On the closing verb he keeps weighed, notes the Hebrew order putting a God of knowledge first, and quotes Rabbi Ami in the Talmud, that knowledge is of great price because it stands between two divine names; he adds that this is one of fifteen places where the Masorites read a negative particle instead as the word meaning by him. Of the reversals he quotes Von Gerlach: every power that will be something in itself is destroyed by the Lord, and every weakness that despairs of itself is transformed into power.

debates.question: Does the closing verb of the third verse mean weighed or directed?

sides.position: directed — by God’s counsel alone can we begin, continue or end any work
weighed — and one of fifteen places where the Masorites correct the particle

themes: there is none holy as the Lord
neither is there any rock like our God
by him actions are weighed
the bows of the mighty men are broken

6.pericope_label: The Lord killeth, and maketh alive

schools.summary: Gill reads a double sense throughout: God removes some by death and preserves others, and of one man can do both, Kimchi and Ben Gersom referring the second clause to the resurrection, while spiritually he kills by the law and quickens by his Spirit. He takes poverty and wealth alike for gifts of providence, the difference between men being contrived so that they depend on one another, and doubles the sense again on the beggar lifted from the dunghill — the literal poor sitting in the dust, and the poor in spirit who alone are beggars, since those who do not feel their want never ask. With the keeping of the saints' feet, he says, the promises begin.

Clarke examines the word rendered grave, which covers the tomb, the state of the dead and the invisible place of spirits; we sometimes render it hell, but since that comes from the Saxon for to conceal it means only the covered place, and the Targum reads a resurrection here. On riches he turns providence into a question of trust: many cannot bear affluence, and if God kept entrusting them with it their ruin would follow, while some he trusts and makes stewards of his secular bounty. He prefers instances to argument, naming three men raised from a dungeon to a throne — Cincinnatus, Joseph and Roushen Akhter, exalted over Hindustan, on whom an elegant couplet was made playing on his name, which means a bright star. Wesley keeps the first clause personal, she who was almost consumed with grief having been revived, notes that death often names a calamity, and glosses the silence of the wicked as a stopping of mouths that once opened wide against heaven.

Ellicott insists that nothing in human affairs is the sport of blind chance, and reports a Talmudic tradition that Hannah's words describe an intermediate class at the judgment, sealed at once neither for life nor for hell, who go down and cry awhile and then ascend. Of the pillars he finds the cosmogony fitted to the childhood of peoples, and adds a rueful question: whether after three or four thousand years, with modern science round us, we know much more of how the universe is made and governed; Jerome rendered the word hinges and Gesenius foundations, but he thinks pillars best. He calls the keeping of the saints' feet the comforting deduction Hannah drew from her own life, set down for the solace of true servants after her, and matches the closing line with the prophet's not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit. On the last verse he makes the strongest claim: this is the first passage in the Old Testament to name his Anointed, Jewish expositors have generally read it of King Messiah, and A Lapide said all these things have regard to Christ. Keil, whose note runs into the next scene, observes that Elkanah then went back to Ramah, the silence about his wives being no warrant for Thenius to send him home alone.

themes: the Lord killeth, and maketh alive
he raiseth up the poor out of the dust
he will keep the feet of his saints
he shall exalt the horn of his anointed

11.pericope_label: Samuel ministered, and the sons of Eli

schools.summary: Gill stresses that the custom was no law of God but a practice the sons introduced, which the other priests followed until it had statutory force. Of the sons themselves he only remarks that they were wicked though they had so good a father.

Henry sets out the design of the passage: two households are interwoven throughout, as if the historian meant to set one against the other, the devotion of Elkanah's family aggravating the iniquity of Eli's, and the sons' wickedness making Samuel's piety shine brighter. Eli's house sat at the tabernacle door, and he draws the moral that the nearer the church the further from God. Nothing appears against Eli himself, who no doubt taught his sons well and prayed for them, yet they grew up profane, which proves that parents cannot give grace to their children nor does it run in the blood; their birth only aggravated the offence, since they lived at the fountain-head of ministry. Of the boy's service he is charmingly concrete: Samuel could light a candle, hold a dish, run an errand or shut a door, and because he did it with a pious mind it is called ministering to the Lord. He notices too, to Israel's honour, that the people, tamely yielding their own rights, were still anxious that God should not be robbed, and begged that the fat be burnt first; it was a shame that priests needed admonishing by the laity.

Clarke calls the sons devil's children, and makes an axiom of it: an impious priesthood is the grand cause of a nation's ruin. He sets the lawful shares against their practice — breast and shoulder to the priest, the fat on the altar, the rest to the offerer — and observes that under pretence of taking their own they took the best and as much as they chose, adding that in demanding raw flesh they would serve themselves before God was served, the priest preferring roast to boiled and lifting it from the pot if he found it there. He traces the effect further: seeing the priests had no piety and acted as though there were no God, the people despised his service. Wesley suggests singing or lighting the lamps as work fit for Samuel's years, and reads before Eli as under his inspection; he adds that the sons snatched their portion even before it was waved, but alone will not let the people off, since the efficacy of the sacraments does not depend on the goodness of those who administer them.

Ellicott corrects a common impression about the name Belial: the English prints it as though it were a pagan deity, but it merely signifies worthlessness, and the capital probably comes from Paul's contrast between Christ and Belial. He quotes Dean Stanley to the effect that the three-pronged fork which fishes up the seething flesh is the earliest type of scrambling after preferment by base means, and the profligacy at the tabernacle door the type of many a later scandal; and he calls the demand for raw flesh a contemptuous insult, the fat being God's portion, so that seizing the flesh first amounted to robbing God. He has Samuel living under the shadow of the sanctuary, ministering with his child powers before the altar of the Invisible and trained by the old high priest. Keil glosses the second clause about the sons to mean they did not know the Lord as he should be known, that is, did not fear him; he says the word rendered custom means a right they had usurped, and quotes Von Gerlach that the robbery was a small sin beside the contempt of the sacrifices they spread among the people.

debates.question: Were the people blameless in coming to abhor the offering?

sides.position: the priests bear it all — seeing them act as though there were no God, the people despised his service
it was folly and sin in the people too, since the sacraments do not depend on those who administer them, though the greater sin lay with the priests

themes: the sons of Eli were sons of Belial
the priest’s custom with the people
men abhorred the offering of the Lord
but Samuel ministered before the Lord

18.pericope_label: The linen ephod and the little coat

schools.summary: Gill explains why the boy's ministry is mentioned both before and after the account of Eli's sons: partly to their shame, partly to Samuel's honour, that he was not corrupted by their practices. He marks a change of phrase too — earlier the child ministered before Eli, under his direction; here before the Lord, in higher services needing no such help — and takes this to belong to a later stage of growth, though related here, while noting that he is still called a child. On the coat he observes that the word is that used for the priest's robe, and that Hannah very likely spun, wove and made it herself, partly from love and partly to lessen the charge of keeping him; the Talmudists allow a priest to minister in a garment his mother made. He adds that Eli pronounced the blessing not only the first time but every year they came up, and that the visitation confirmed it.

Clarke leaves the garment for the word, reporting that the Targum renders it a cardit of byssus, a term apparently borrowed from the Greek for a sleeved tunic the Romans thought effeminate. He is practical about the coat, calling it a cloak or surtout to keep the boy from the cold and save his other clothes from being spoiled in his meaner services, and supposes a new one each year. Alone among them he thinks the passage disordered, the natural place of the blessing seeming to him before the eleventh verse, with the twenty-first following and perhaps the twenty-sixth after, the subjects of the chapter being much entangled by the wrong position of the verses. Wesley reads the verb as discharging his office faithfully and the place as the tabernacle, alone raises the difficulty of who might wear the ephod, and closes on the boy, who grew not only in age and stature but in wisdom and goodness, and grew so before the Lord, not merely before men, who may be deceived, but under an all-seeing eye.

Keil calls the ephod a shoulder-dress resembling the high priest's in shape but made of plain white cloth; all the priests wore such then, and David wore one at a religious festival, Samuel receiving it as a boy because he was set apart to a lifelong service. He takes the coat for a smaller version of the high priest's robe, of simpler stuff and without the symbolical ornaments on the hem, paraphrases the blessing as asking that the Lord lend Elkanah seed of this woman in place of the one asked for, and explains its odd third person as indefinite, since Eli might fairly assume the father shared Hannah's desire. Against Clarke he insists that the particle joining the blessing to its fulfilment is neither a conditional nor a copyist's error, one need only supply the thought that Eli's word was no empty wish. Ellicott finds a deliberate contrast between the covetous ministrations of the worldly priests and the quiet service of the boy, describes the ephod as two pieces resting on the shoulders before and behind, joined at the top and fastened with a girdle, and looks past the cloth to the intention, taking the dress to have been arranged by Eli, who saw the child destined for some great work and, aware what his own sons were, hoped to train him as his successor in the chief office in Israel.

outliers.claim: holds the chapter’s verses to stand in the wrong order — the blessing belongs before the eleventh verse, with the twenty-first following and perhaps the twenty-sixth after that
allows the ephod to Samuel not as a priest or Levite but as one of the eminent persons among the people, he being a Nazarite

themes: girded with a linen ephod
his mother made him a little coat
Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife
the Lord visited Hannah

schools.summary: Gill reckons Eli about ninety, since he died at ninety-eight, and thinks the note shows his incapacity for office, which gave his sons their chance; it also accounts for the gentleness of the reproof, age having left him less spirit and his sons being grown. Yet he will not let that stand as a defence: Eli ought to have considered himself not a father only but high priest and judge. The sins deserved a sharper reprimand and worse than words, and Gill objects even to the address, my sons being too endearing for men who deserved the name of Belial. He notes at the close that Samuel grew better while Eli's sons grew worse, the contrast making one shine and the other look blacker.

Clarke supposes the women had some employment about the sanctuary, citing the same phrase in Exodus, and draws Eli's character: a fondly affectionate, easy father who wished his sons well but never brought them under discipline nor used his authority to restrain them, though as judge he could have cast them out at once. On the unanswerable question he turns to the gospel, since the law fixed which sins were capital and allowed no appeal, whereas John writes that if any man sin we have an Advocate with the Father. He then rejects the closing construction as a mistranslation: the particle rendered because should be rendered therefore, as Noldius takes it here, so that it was their not hearkening which induced the Lord to will their destruction. Wesley states the fault precisely — the sin was not only that he reproved too gently but that he rested in a rebuke and inflicted none of the punishments such crimes deserved — and says they had sinned away their day of grace and hardened their hearts, till God gave them up.

Keil observes that the crime is learned only from the reproof itself, so that beside robbing the offerings they profaned the sanctuary with whoredom, and that this whole people means everyone who came to Shiloh and saw. He notes a play in the Hebrew that cannot be carried over, the verb meaning to decide a case, then to arbitrate, then in another form to entreat, so that when a man sins against man God settles the dispute through the authorities, but when a man sins against God none can interpose. Ellicott hears something warmer in the note about Eli's age, holding that the compiler plainly wished to speak as kindly of him as he could, dwelling on his piety, his love for Samuel and his patriotism, so that here, where his sons' conduct is at its worst, an excuse is offered for the father. He thinks the women may have assisted in the liturgy, comparing the psalm about the great company of female singers, and adds that here, as so often, immorality follows on unbelief; the unanswerable question he says touches the mystery of sin, one transgression seeming to lie beyond forgiveness, of which the Redeemer warned as the sin against the Holy Ghost. Of the closing clause he takes the resolution to slay them as founded on the eternal foreknowledge of their persistence, a period coming in a sinner's life when the Spirit ceases to plead and he is left to himself.

debates.question: Why would Eli’s sons not hear their father?

sides.position: God’s resolution to slay them rested on his eternal foreknowledge of their persistence in wrong-doing
they had sinned away their day of grace and were at last given up
the particle is mistranslated — read therefore, not because: their not hearkening induced the Lord to will their destruction

themes: why do ye such things?
ye make the Lord’s people to transgress
if a man sin against the Lord, who shall intreat for him?
they hearkened not, because the Lord would slay them

27.pericope_label: The man of God comes to Eli

schools.summary: Gill canvasses the candidates for the unnamed prophet: Ben Gersom and Abarbinel propose Phinehas, impossible, since had he lived Eli would not have been high priest; the older Jews and Jarchi name Elkanah, whom the Targum makes a disciple of the prophets, though Scripture never calls him one; others suggest Samuel, concealing his name from modesty, but he was still a child. On the charge of kicking he hears a metaphor from cattle well fed and fat, which spurn even those who feed them, and reports the Targum's harder reading, that they took the holy offerings by force.

Henry explains why the message came, and why to the father rather than the sons: Eli had reproved too gently, so God sent a prophet to reprove him sharply, and sent it to Eli because he meant to save him, having already determined to destroy his sons. If good men fail in their duty and by their remissness contribute to the sin of sinners, they must expect both to hear of it and to smart for it. He sums the recital of past favours as an aggravation: what more could God have done to engage them, and such favours will be remembered against us if we profane our crown.

Clarke traces the office from Aaron to Eleazar and Phinehas, then into the younger branch, and back again because of the profligacy of Eli's sons. He holds the pledge of a perpetual priesthood, though it looks absolute, to be conditional like all such promises, the condition implied though not expressed, so that unworthy walking annuls it; but the rule which follows he calls a plan from which God never departs, underlying every promise — them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed. Wesley reads the charge of honouring sons above God as connivance, Eli choosing rather to offend God by his silence than to displease them, and states flatly that God retracts what he promised.

Ellicott declines the guessing about the prophet's identity: this messenger appears suddenly at Shiloh, nameless and homeless, delivers his doom, and disappears; the title occurs some forty times in Judges, Samuel and Kings, and no prophet had been named in Israel's story since Deborah. The opening interrogations, he says, ask nothing but appeal to Eli's conscience, the old man answering each with a silent yes. He traces the image of kicking to the song of Moses, where Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked, a pampered beast growing unmanageable and refusing obedience to a kind master, and suspects a second motive in Eli besides foolish fondness: unwillingness to divert from his family the rich revenue flowing from the pilgrims' offerings. Keil sets out the three clauses defining the priesthood — to ascend the altar, to kindle incense, to wear the ephod — and observes that the reproof falls first on the priests generally, Eli included, since he had not resisted the abuses, and narrows to him only in the words about honouring his sons.

debates.question: What did the promise that Eli’s house should walk before God for ever mean?

sides.position: an apparently absolute promise that was conditional all along, annulled by unworthy walking
not a transfer of the high priesthood to Ithamar’s line at all — the promise ran to the whole priesthood, against C. a Lapide

themes: thus saith the Lord unto the house of thy father
wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice?
thou honourest thy sons above me
them that honour me I will honour

31.pericope_label: The judgment on the house of Eli

schools.summary: Gill notes that the threat took effect quickly, in the days of Eli's sons, and was complete in eighty years. Of the enemy in the habitation he prefers the rival reading, of Solomon's time, when Abiathar of Eli's family was thrust out and Zadok put in; and he names Zadok as the faithful priest, rejecting Samuel, who was not of the priestly race and had no sure house, his sons having declined from the ways of truth.

Clarke observes that almost every version and commentator takes the clause about the enemy differently. He reads the word as calamity rather than rival, finding it in the defeat of Israel, the capture of the ark and the death of his sons, all known to Eli before his own tragical end. He agrees with Gill on Zadok, and turns the last verse into a warning, since they who once fed to the full on the Lord's sacrifices now beg a morsel of bread. Wesley canvasses what the arm was — the ark, called God's strength in the psalm and Eli's too, since he could not bear the news of its loss; or his priestly dignity; or, likeliest, his children — reads the enemy as the affliction of the sanctuary, puts the flower of their age at about thirty, and finds Christ in the anointed before whom the priest walks, the high priest being a type who went before him as John afterwards did.

Keil explains that a family's strength lies in the vital energy of its members, showing itself in their reaching a good old age instead of pining away early; that would now fail. On the habitation he takes a third course: in all the benefits conferred on his people Eli would see only distress for the dwelling, the tabernacle falling further into decay; and since the high priest is addressed as custodian, the words bind his whole house. He pairs the next threat's clauses with the thoughts before: someone of Eli's family would always serve at the altar, precisely so that he might watch the decay and pine away. He reports Ephraem Syrus taking both candidates for the faithful priest, Samuel succeeding to the government and Zadok to the office, and glosses the coin as a small piece got by begging singly. Ellicott adds that sickness or the sword would consume the members young, weighs the rival readings of the enemy and prefers the ark, whose loss robbed the earthly habitation of the Eternal of its glory, and points to the last verse for the sense of the threat: those not cut off in youth would be worse off than those who were, since they must beg their bread.

debates.question: Who is the faithful priest God will raise up?

sides.position: Zadok, put into the office by Solomon in Abiathar’s room
Samuel, who succeeded Eli in his functions and walked before the anointed Saul — and Zadok is too obscure a man for such magnificent promises
both, Samuel succeeding to the government and Zadok to the priesthood

outliers.claim: refuses those who find Christ in the faithful priest, since this priest is to walk before the Lord’s Anointed — where Wesley finds Christ exactly

themes: I will cut off thine arm
thou shalt see an enemy in my habitation
in one day they shall die both of them
I will raise me up a faithful priest
